Phase B wire-in is justified.

Phase A control — same Sonnet, same diplomatic-transcript instructions including no-fabrication clause, but reading the full 911x8313 PNG. Fabricated extensively despite the explicit instructions: 'T. P. PAIGE' for $5 REWARD signature (actual JAS. L. C. MORE), 'W. T. PAIGE' for store ad (actual R. F. NAGLE), 'WHITE LANE' (actual WHITE LAKE), '90 CENTS EACH' (actual 20), 'Flowers in Endless Variety, Stamped and Japanese Ware' (actual Tinware/Japanned Ware), garbled 'WEAV SIC, DOE DOOR' for the Crossley ad. The model honestly noted in transcriber_notes that it was working at downsampled resolution and could not read body text — yet still emitted plausible names where it could not read them. Confirms: the no-fabrication rule is necessary but not sufficient when the image is downsampled. Slicing is the structural fix.

Phase A second comparison — Haiku on the same 12 h-rule-bounded slices. RESULT: matches the Opus v3 benchmark on every previously-fabricated fact (MACDONELL & STAFFORD, JAS. L. C. MORE, JOHN SCOTT, R. F. NAGLE, PANMURE, WHITE LAKE, 20 CENTS EACH, Tinware/Japanned Ware). Slicing fixes the fabrication mode regardless of model. Quality differences vs Sonnet sliced: Haiku misread '$35.00' for the new Top Buggy where benchmark + Sonnet both have '$85.00' (single-digit OCR slip, 3 vs 8); missed the printed manicule ☞ in slices 4/6/8 and emitted '---' instead — would inject false rule markers if the orchestrator joined naively; did not flag the within-slice h-rule on slice 9 (above FACTS FOR ALL) that Sonnet caught; did not hedge the ambiguous '1[?b]' issue character at the masthead; included masthead 'Almonte.' bleed at top of slices 0 and 4 instead of ignoring the overlap as instructed. Bonus: preserved the Phæton ligature (Sonnet wrote 'Phaeton'). Net: Haiku is viable for clean structural facts on sliced inputs; Sonnet remains stronger on edge cases, hesitation markers, and printer's-mark recognition. Production default stays Sonnet; Haiku is a candidate for cheap-and-clean classified columns later.

Correction, prompted by user pushback (do not just give up on the image-read batching question). The ~10s/column batching-savings claim used all day (in the audit, in the column-transcriber.md prose, in the ~29-days-at-scale estimate) was INHERITED from the pre-existing instructions text -- I never independently measured it before building a finding and a fix around it. Generation gap (last Read to Write) was 129-295s -- two orders of magnitude larger. This means: (1) the true ceiling on batching savings is ~2-3s/column (the inter-call round-trip overhead), not ~10s -- at 250K columns thats ~7 days, not ~29; (2) since batching does not even work via prompt engineering (confirmed falsified separately), this ~7-day ceiling remains entirely unrealized and is not worth further engineering effort chasing given both its now-small size and its resistance to the fix already tried; (3) the dominant cost by two orders of magnitude is the generation/transcription phase itself (130-295s), not the read phase -- if further wall-clock optimization is wanted, that is where it would need to focus, and that is a much harder problem (content difficulty, self-check depth) already partially characterized by the earlier end-of-issue slowdown investigation. The self-timing cascade estimate (~52 days at scale) is NOT affected by this correction -- that one was grounded in directly-counted real Bash-call data (322 timing-related calls across 88 agents) plus real observed retry durations (3.2-8.6s range from actual transcripts), and is cross-validated by the tests own observed ~12s/column real duration drop after self-timing was removed.

Direct self-test per user request (time yourself reading all slices at once vs one at a time), to cross-check the subagent-transcript-derived ~3.2-3.5s total read-phase finding. Read the same 4 real slice images (920x2500px newspaper column scans) two ways: batched (4 Read calls in one tool-call block) timed at 9.70s; sequential (4 separate Read calls, each its own turn) timed at 22.37s -- a real, directly-measured ~12.7s difference, much closer to the original ~10s estimate than the subagent data suggested. Reconciliation: this test ran in the main sessions own (very large, heavily-loaded) context, not a fresh subagent context (confirmed via the earlier prompt-caching investigation to be ~13K tokens for a fresh dispatch). Larger context plausibly means more per-turn overhead, so batching saves more here than for a subagent with little per-turn overhead to begin with -- a coherent explanation, not a contradiction. Net conclusion: batching read calls IS a real, verified technique with measurable benefit in general, but its payoff for THIS specific pipelines subagents appears to be genuinely small (~3.2-3.5s total either way per the transcript data) because those agents already run in small fresh contexts. The self-test result and its caveat are being added to the document rather than treated as a reason to re-open the batching-fix chase, since the two pieces of evidence together, not either alone, give the complete picture.

Per user pushback (make a subagent to run the test), redid the batched-vs-sequential comparison as two real subagent dispatches (general-purpose, both starting by reading column-transcriber.md for realistic context size), each reading 4 fresh, size-matched slice sets (222KB vs 259KB) neither had seen before. Result: batched=9.79s, sequential=17.14s -- a real ~7.4s gap, controlled for context size and image novelty, closer to the original ~10s estimate than the production-transcript findings ~3.2-3.5s. BUT: extracted precise timestamps and found why -- the sequential agent showed GROWING deliberation gaps before each read (2.19s, 2.56s, 3.30s, 3.46s), while the batched agent showed tiny gaps throughout (0.09-0.44s). The sequential agent was explicitly instructed to read one at a time, each its own separate turn -- that specific instruction appears to have taught it to pace/deliberate between reads, an artifact of the test design itself, not a property of unbatched reading. Real production agents are never told to slow down; they just do not comply with the batching ask, and their transcripts (wf_87bc9020-b8c) show tiny gaps throughout regardless, totaling only ~3.2-3.5s. CONCLUSION: the production-transcript number (~3.2-3.5s total, batched or not) is the most trustworthy figure for this pipelines actual behavior, since it is the only one free of an injected instruction-pacing bias. Both controlled self-tests were individually informative (confirmed batching CAN save real time under some conditions) but each carried its own confound (session context size; explicit pacing instruction) that does not apply to real dispatches. Net: read-phase cost for this pipeline remains small next to the 130-295s generation phase regardless of which measurement is used.

Rewrote column-transcriber.md for token efficiency, per user request and user-demonstrated tightening style (compact phrasing, caps for emphasis, cut illustrative-but-non-essential examples, imperative over descriptive phrasing). 29,258 -> 18,396 bytes (37.1pct reduction, ~7,314 -> ~4,599 est. tokens). This applies per-dispatch regardless of any caching/batching work -- ~2,700 fewer tokens on every single column, no structural/quality risk since behavior is unchanged, only wording. Changes: (1) removed meta-commentary/changelog-style asides that documented WHY a rule exists for future human readers but arent needed by the agent (the "measured 2026-08-06..." timing justification, the self-timing-removal changelog parenthetical); (2) consolidated the "dont use PIL/dont zoom" rule from 3 restatements to 1; (3) shrank the ad-cross-check section (~69 lines) while preserving all 6 distinct rules -- checked against 200 real tickets: masked field, unregistered-ad, ad-spanning-columns, and article-vs-ad-fragment leniency rules all kept; (4) shrank the full-image-mode appendix (~40 lines) to a compact fallback note -- checked all 2,206 tickets currently on disk, 0pct are full-image mode, so this section costs every real dispatch and helps none of them; (5) tightened prose throughout (input-modes overview, self-check bullets, notes-discipline examples, quality_flags/repair_kind definitions) while preserving every distinct behavioral rule. Did NOT touch: the do-not-invent-text rule, marker syntax definitions ([illegible]/[?word]/etc, kept verbatim -- exact syntax matters), the self-check pass, the response JSON schema (both code blocks re-validated as parseable JSON after the edit), or any quality_flags/repair_kind field names or criteria. Verified: both JSON schema blocks parse as valid JSON; all 16 section headers preserved; every marker/field-name/enum-value from the original confirmed still present in the new text via automated grep check. Not yet tested against a live dispatch -- next production or small validation batch is the first real test that trimmed prose didnt lose any behavioral nuance in practice (as opposed to just surviving a keyword-presence check).

Implemented and verified the agentType tool-restriction fix in transcribe_continuous.js: tier1Prompt and tier2SlicePrompt dispatches now pass agentType: "column-transcriber" instead of a plain workflow-subagent call, and tier1Prompt no longer tells the agent to explicitly Read .claude/agents/column-transcriber.md (confirmed unnecessary -- the registered agent type bakes the current file content into the system prompt directly). Verified via two rounds of live testing: (1) a single direct Agent-tool dispatch (subagent_type: column-transcriber) -- 0 deferred-tool attachments vs 82 before, no explicit agent-file Read, correct ingest with working confidence field; (2) a 5-column batch through the actual production Workflow path -- same 0-attachment result across all 5 agents, PLUS an unplanned bonus: 2 of 5 agents landed close enough in time to share prompt cache across independent conversations (cache_read=14,674 on their own first turn despite zero shared context), since agentType makes every dispatch's system prompt byte-identical. This is opportunistic/timing-dependent (2/5 not 5/5 here), not guaranteed, but real and free -- achieves part of the caching benefit the multi-column-batching proposal was chasing, without any of its quality risk, since each column is still a fully independent conversation. Turn-1 baseline dropped from ~28.6K tokens (13.5K read-batch + 15.1K fixed tool overhead) to ~23.4K (sometimes ~9K when cache lands). 3 of 5 test columns hit content-filter blocks in the production-path test -- confirmed NOT a regression: 4/6 columns on the same page succeeded cleanly via the identical new pathway, and the 2 failures (adjacent columns, both blocked on the same slice index) show the exact signature of one specific passage tripping the classifier, which the existing Tier-1->2->manual-3/4 ladder caught and flagged correctly. Also checked and ruled out: trimming drive_id/drive_url/image_sha256/prompt_hash out of the ticket the agent reads -- prompt_hash is read independently by the ingester from the ticket file on disk, so it must stay; total savings from dropping unused fields would be ~60 tokens, not worth a dual-ticket-file structure. transcribe_continuous.js snapshot synced to instructions/transcribe_continuous.js.snapshot.
